sections.h2: What is the STAR program in New York?
sections.html:
STAR is the School Tax Relief program, and it cuts the school tax on a house that the owner lives in as a primary residence. It comes in two levels: Basic STAR for any age, and Enhanced STAR for owners 65 and older with lower incomes.

The benefit reaches you in one of two forms. The STAR credit is a check or direct deposit from the state that you use to pay the school bill. The STAR exemption is a cut taken off the school bill itself. According to the Tax Department's eligibility page, the exemption is closed to new homeowners, while people who have received it since 2015 can keep it on the same primary residence.

For a seller, that split matters. If your house carries the exemption, your buyer will not inherit it, and a buyer who needs the benefit has to register for the credit.

STAR reduces school district taxes only. The Tax Department says it does not touch county, town or village bills, with one exception: in New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse the benefit is split between city taxes and school taxes.

Many owners expect a larger drop than they get for this reason. A homeowner outside those five cities will see the savings only on the school portion of the combined tax statement. Senior citizens who receive STAR may also qualify for a separate senior citizens exemption, which is a separate program. Ask your local assessor how to apply for it.

sections.h2: What are the Basic and Enhanced STAR income limits?
sections.html:
Basic STAR has an income limit of $500,000 for the credit and $250,000 for the exemption, and it applies to the first $30,000 of a home's full value. Enhanced STAR is open to owners 65 and older with income of $110,750 or less for the 2026-27 school year and $113,550 or less for 2027-28.

Income means federal adjusted gross income minus the taxable part of IRA distributions. The 2026 benefit is judged on the 2024 tax year, and the income counted belongs to resident owners and their resident spouses. Income of owners who do not live in the home is left out.

sections.h2: Who is eligible to receive STAR?
sections.html:
You must own the property, live in it as your primary residence, and meet the age and income test for the level you want. For a credit in any given year, you need to own the home and live in it as of July 1 of that year.

  • Houses, condominiums, cooperative apartments, manufactured homes and farm houses can qualify.
  • A married couple gets only one STAR benefit, however many properties they own, unless they are legally separated.
  • Someone buying under a land contract (an executory contract of sale) counts as an owner.
  • Corporations, partnerships and LLCs are not eligible unless the property is a farm dwelling.
  • A nursing home resident who owns the home can still qualify if no one besides a co-owner or spouse lives there.

The state looks at how long you spend at the property each year, where you are registered to vote, and the address on your vehicle registrations and government IDs. The Tax Department can ask for proof of residency.

sections.h2: How do trusts, life estates and surviving spouses fit in?
sections.html:
A person who put the home in a trust but still lives there as the trust beneficiary is treated as the owner and gets the STAR benefit. Under a life estate, the life tenant is deemed the owner for STAR purposes, so eligibility turns on the life tenant's own age and income.

A surviving spouse can keep an Enhanced STAR benefit earned by the late spouse if the survivor reaches 62 by December 31 of the year of death. A younger survivor receives Basic STAR until turning 65 and then moves to Enhanced STAR if otherwise eligible.

These cases come up after a death in the family. If you are handling an inherited house, check how title is held before you list it, because a change of ownership means the STAR registration should be updated or closed.

sections.h2: How do you register for the STAR credit?
sections.html:
You register once through the Homeowner Benefit Portal inside your Individual Online Services account with the Tax Department. After logging in, open the Services menu, choose Real property tax, then Homeowner Benefit Portal, and select Register.

Have these items ready before you begin:

  • names and Social Security numbers for all owners and their spouses
  • the name of your school district and the approximate purchase date
  • the most recent school tax bill, if the current owners received one
  • 2024 federal or state income tax returns for all owners
  • the legal name of the trust, if one holds title

Sellers' names are optional but can help you receive the credit before school taxes come due. Write down the confirmation number, because the Tax Department will ask for it if you call. If you pay school tax through a mortgage escrow account, tell the lender or its agent when you switch from the exemption to the credit.

sections.h2: What should you do with your STAR registration when you sell?
sections.html:
Close it. The Tax Department says that if you sell the property or no longer want the benefit, you should close the registration from the Homeowner Benefit Portal. You do not register again each year, and the state reviews your information annually and issues the credit automatically when you remain eligible.

Update the registration instead of closing it if ownership changes through marriage, divorce, a co-owner giving up an interest, survivorship, a trust, a life estate or a name change.

Buyers have their own task. A new owner who is not yet receiving STAR should register as soon as the house becomes the primary residence, and the Tax Department publishes a one-page handout for realtors and attorneys to give to purchasers. Ask the assessor in your county whether any local exemption on the house is removed at sale, since local exemptions are handled separately from STAR.

sections.h2: What happens to STAR and other exemptions at a closing?
sections.html:
STAR stays with the owner who registered, so it does not pass to the buyer through the deed. The state-level step is simple: the seller closes the registration and the buyer registers for the credit.

Local exemptions work through the county. Take Nassau County's North Hempstead as an example: the town's closing guide says exemptions are generally not transferable at closing and that buyers should apply with the county Department of Assessment. It also warns that when an exemption is removed after a sale, the county may add prorated restored taxes to a later bill, up to one year's worth, and that this can take up to two years to appear.

The practical lesson holds across the state. Before you sign, ask your closing attorney or the county assessor which exemptions are on the house, and ask whether a restored-tax charge could follow the sale. A buyer who is counting on the exemption in the price should hear the answer before the contract is final.

faqs.q: Can a new buyer get the STAR exemption on a house in New York?
faqs.a: No. The exemption is closed to new homeowners, and the Tax Department says people who have received it since 2015 can continue only for the same primary residence. A buyer registers for the STAR credit once the house is their primary residence.

faqs.q: Do I need to register for STAR every year?
faqs.a: No. You register once, and the Tax Department issues the credit each year as long as you stay eligible. You only update the registration when ownership changes, and you close it if you sell.

faqs.q: What is the Enhanced STAR income limit for 2027-28?
faqs.a: It is $113,550 or less. For the 2026-27 school year the limit is $110,750, and at least one resident owner must be 65 or older by December 31 of the benefit year.

faqs.q: Does STAR lower my county or town tax?
faqs.a: No. It applies only to school district taxes, except in New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse, where the benefit is applied partly to city taxes and partly to school taxes.

faqs.q: Can an LLC or a corporation receive STAR?
faqs.a: No, unless the property is a farm dwelling. The state limits the benefit to eligible individual owners who live in the home, and a trust beneficiary who lives there is treated as the owner.
